cse-1994-a-1.approach: Recursion needs a fresh activation record per call; classic FORTRAN binds every local variable to one fixed (static) storage location at compile time, so a second active call would overwrite the first.

steps.title: What recursion needs
steps.body: Each active invocation of a procedure needs its **own** copy of locals, parameters and return address — i.e. a new activation record per call, normally on a stack.

steps.title: What FORTRAN does
steps.body: Classic FORTRAN (FORTRAN 77 and earlier) uses **static allocation**: every variable of a subprogram has a single address fixed at compile/link time. A recursive call would reuse — and overwrite — the caller's locals and return address, so recursion is disallowed.

Dynamic (stack/heap) allocation is exactly what *enables* recursion, so it cannot be the reason it is forbidden.

Recursion can be implemented on any machine with addressable memory; the limitation is the language's storage model.

pitfalls: Confusing 'no hardware stack' with 'no recursion' — a software stack suffices.

cse-1994-a-20.approach: Call-by-name re-evaluates the actual-parameter expression at every use; call-by-reference binds its address once. They differ only when the argument's address can change during the call — e.g. `a[i]` when `i` is modified.
